Prediction target period: from 2025-01-08 to 2025-01-23. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A market report published on January 3, 2025, indicated that the U.S. butter market is anticipated to sustain its strength through the early part of the year. [2] This stability is attributed to a combination of steady consumer demand and tighter supplies. [2] The supply constraints are influenced by a significant reduction in Cold Storage inventories during late 2024 and sustained high demand over the holiday season. [2] One analyst also noted that lower dairy production in California has contributed to the tighter supplies. [2] <2> An outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) across California's dairy herds led to a historic 9.2% year-over-year drop in the state's milk production for November 2024, the most significant decrease since 1950. [8] The number of affected herds grew rapidly, from 203 on November 1 to 645 by December 17, prompting the state's governor to declare a state of emergency. [7, 8] While the reduced milk supply in the nation's largest dairy state raised concerns about the availability and cost of dairy products into 2025, national butter production paradoxically increased. [8] One source reported that California's butter production specifically saw a 13% year-over-year decline. [9] However, nationally, total butter production rose by 4.4% in November to 171 million pounds, as producers in other regions appeared to increase output, potentially to meet holiday demand. [6, 9] <3> The dairy industry is expected to conclude 2024 with fluctuating butter and cheese prices. A report from December 18, 2024, highlighted a decrease in the prices of key dairy commodities, with USDA data showing butter prices falling by 14.60 cents per pound and Cheddar cheese dropping by over 17 cents per pound. This price reduction is projected to make U.S. dairy products more competitive and appealing in international markets, partly due to favorable exchange rates. <4> In the final months of 2024, the U.S. dairy market saw a divergence between wholesale and retail butter prices. Wholesale prices experienced a significant drop, falling by 54 cents to a low of $2.65 per pound by October 7, 2024, which in turn impacted Class IV milk prices for dairy farmers. Despite this wholesale decline, consumer prices for butter remained high heading into the holiday season, as reported on December 17, 2024. This price disparity at the retail level occurred even as domestic demand for butter remained strong. <5> In the fourth quarter of 2024, the U.S. dairy market experienced a significant butter surplus. Butter production in October totaled 167 million pounds, a 3.1% increase compared to the previous year, contributing to a notable rise in inventories. [2, 12] By October 31, butter stocks reached 267.5 million pounds, which is an 11.4% increase year-over-year and the highest level for that date since 2021. [2, 5] This surplus occurred despite a reported 4% growth in domestic butter demand for the year. [2] <6> A report from the USDA's Economic Research Service confirmed a significant long-term trend of increasing butter consumption in the U.S. [1] In 2023, per capita butter consumption rose to a record 6.5 pounds, a 0.4-pound increase from the previous year. [2, 4] This figure reflects a sustained strong consumer demand for butter, which has seen consumption grow by 18% over the last decade. [1, 2] <7> A market report published on October 27, 2024, stated that the United States Salted Butter market was valued at US$ 4.85 billion in 2024. The report projects the market will reach US$ 5.95 billion by 2030. It also highlighted a 35% expansion in export markets, with Canada being the primary destination. <8> On October 16, 2024, the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) dairy markets experienced a notable surge in demand for butter. The price for butter rose by two cents to $2.6350 per pound amidst heavy trading, which included record trade volumes. This increase in both price and volume indicated robust market demand, presenting potential opportunities for producers to increase production. While the butter market showed strength, other cash dairy prices on the CME were mixed on the same day. <9> In early October 2024, the U.S. butter market saw a significant price drop, with spot prices falling by 54¢ to $2.65 per pound as of October 7, 2024, the lowest price since late January. [2] This decline followed a period of high summer prices that had surpassed $3.00 per pound. [2] The downturn was attributed to a robust domestic supply, evidenced by a 4.8% increase in butter production over the first eight months of the year. [2] Furthermore, substantial inventory levels, which reached 323.284 million pounds by the end of August—a 10.8% increase from the previous year—indicated a market surplus. [2] The more competitive U.S. prices were seen as creating potential new opportunities for American butter exports on the global stage. [2] <10> A retrospective market analysis indicates that U.S. butter prices on the CME spot market consistently remained above $3 per pound for a significant portion of the summer of 2024, a trend that began when prices first crossed that threshold on May 1. This period of elevated prices culminated in late August, with the spot price reaching a high of $3.1975 per pound on August 31, 2024. Following this peak, the market saw a dramatic downturn, with prices falling significantly as increased domestic production and substantial inventories created a surplus.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> US dairy markets experienced a simultaneous drop across every major exchange, signaling a real-time reset of the global dairy industry. During this broad decline, CME Cheddar blocks fell to $1.345 per pound—their lowest level since July 2023—while butter markets continued a steep crash into the $1.50 per pound range driven by a structural oversupply of domestic butterfat. <2> The USDA released its December World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report, projecting lower consumer dairy product prices for 2026. Specifically, the report forecasted that U.S. consumer butter prices would fall from $2.22 per pound to approximately $1.67 per pound. <3> At the Global Dairy Trade (GDT) auction, butter prices plummeted by 12.4% as part of a broader 4.3% decline in the GDT price index. This sharp drop was heavily influenced by global buyers shifting their procurement to the United States. Throughout 2025, U.S. butter prices have been significantly discounted compared to European and New Zealand markets, prompting buyers to capitalize on the value of American products, which consequently gained market share in regions like Asia and the Middle East. <4> Weekly wholesale butter prices from the Chicago Mercantile Exchange showed significant volatility throughout October 2025, rather than a continued decline. After a sharp price drop early in the month, which saw prices fall to $1.6025, the price for Grade AA butter ended the month at $1.6100 per pound on October 31, 2025. Reports from early October noted a collapse in the butter price to around $1.60 per pound. <5> In early October 2025, reports confirmed that U.S. butter prices had fallen to their lowest level in four years, with spot prices dropping to as low as $1.6025 per pound. The significant price decline was attributed to high milk output and a surplus of cream heading into the autumn baking season. Contributing factors included an increase in the national dairy herd by 176,000 cows compared to the previous year and a 1.7% rise in milk-per-cow production in September. This oversupply led to a fundamental shift in dairy component values, with the discount on spot butter loads reaching levels not seen since 2020. <6> In mid-September 2025, multiple reports confirmed that U.S. butter prices had fallen to a three to four-year low, with butter futures plunging by approximately 28-30% since July. This significant price drop was attributed to a butter glut caused by near-record seasonal production outpacing demand. Specifically, July's butter production exceeded 180 million pounds, the highest for that month in over a decade, according to the Department of Agriculture. The oversupply stems from record-high butterfat levels in milk, a result of advances in dairy farm genetics and animal nutrition. While demand for butter remains strong, with U.S. exports surging, the sheer volume of production has continued to pressure prices. <7> The USDA's September 2025 World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report, released on September 12, 2025, increased the milk production forecast for both 2025 and 2026. This upward revision was attributed to a larger dairy herd and higher milk output per cow. As a result of the anticipated increase in supply, the USDA lowered its all-milk price forecasts for both years. The projected average all-milk price for 2025 is $21.35 per hundredweight, and the forecast for 2026 is $20.40 per hundredweight. <8> On July 23, 2025, CME spot butter prices experienced a significant drop of nearly 6 cents, settling at $2.42 per pound. [1] This event, part of a broader return to the $2.40/lb range in late July, was attributed to a readily available supply of butter. The increased availability stemmed from several major butter plants resuming operations after extended maintenance, boosting supply at a time when demand was showing signs of weakening. This price drop is considered part of a midyear reset for U.S. dairy prices, which could enhance the affordability of U.S. dairy products on the global market. However, some market analysis suggests that many producers were viewing the downturn as temporary market noise rather than a fundamental shift. [1] <9> In its World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report released on July 11, 2025, the USDA raised its all-milk price forecast for 2025 to $22.00 per hundredweight, a slight increase of five cents from the previous month's projection. This adjustment is based on higher forecasts for milk cow inventories and an increased rate of growth in milk per cow. The report cited expectations of favorable farm margins and robust demand for U.S. dairy products as contributing factors. Specifically, price forecasts for butter, nonfat dry milk (NDM), and whey were increased due to strong demand. However, the cheese price forecast was lowered because of recent price data and increased production capacity, which in turn slightly lowered the Class III milk price forecast.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> CME spot butter prices remained depressed into the new year, with prices recorded around $1.41 to $1.43 per pound in late January 2026. This ongoing price slump represents a roughly 40% decline over a six-month period, dropping from $2.60 per pound in mid-July of the previous year. <2> On January 29, 2026, during a 2026 market outlook discussion on the Hoard's Dairyman podcast, Terrain Ag's senior dairy economist, Ben Laine, and CoBank's lead dairy economist, Corey Geiger, highlighted a unique market dynamic. They noted that a sustained crash in U.S. butter prices inversely drove significant strength in the protein values paid to dairy producers on their milk checks. <3> DecisionNext published an analysis revealing that the correlation between the expanding U.S. milking herd size and falling butter prices reached its most pronounced divergence in two decades during the 2025 market crash. <4> US dairy markets experienced a simultaneous drop across every major exchange, signaling a real-time reset of the global dairy industry. During this broad decline, CME Cheddar blocks fell to $1.345 per pound—their lowest level since July 2023—while butter markets continued a steep crash into the $1.50 per pound range driven by a structural oversupply of domestic butterfat. <5> The USDA released its December World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report, projecting lower consumer dairy product prices for 2026. Specifically, the report forecasted that U.S. consumer butter prices would fall from $2.22 per pound to approximately $1.67 per pound. <6> At the Global Dairy Trade (GDT) auction, butter prices plummeted by 12.4% as part of a broader 4.3% decline in the GDT price index. This sharp drop was heavily influenced by global buyers shifting their procurement to the United States. Throughout 2025, U.S. butter prices have been significantly discounted compared to European and New Zealand markets, prompting buyers to capitalize on the value of American products, which consequently gained market share in regions like Asia and the Middle East. <7> Weekly wholesale butter prices from the Chicago Mercantile Exchange showed significant volatility throughout October 2025, rather than a continued decline. After a sharp price drop early in the month, which saw prices fall to $1.6025, the price for Grade AA butter ended the month at $1.6100 per pound on October 31, 2025. Reports from early October noted a collapse in the butter price to around $1.60 per pound. <8> In early October 2025, reports confirmed that U.S. butter prices had fallen to their lowest level in four years, with spot prices dropping to as low as $1.6025 per pound. The significant price decline was attributed to high milk output and a surplus of cream heading into the autumn baking season. Contributing factors included an increase in the national dairy herd by 176,000 cows compared to the previous year and a 1.7% rise in milk-per-cow production in September. This oversupply led to a fundamental shift in dairy component values, with the discount on spot butter loads reaching levels not seen since 2020.
